text: François Aimé Louis Dumoulin (French pronunciation: [fʁɑ̃swa eme lwi dymulɛ̃]; 10 August 1753 – 16 February 1834) was a Swiss painter and engraver. Although he received some education in technical drawing, he was initially intended for a commercial career. In 1772, he sailed to England and traveled to America the following year. Upon arriving in Grenada, he engaged in business while drawing plans and views for the governor. From 1776 to 1782, Dumoulin witnessed the American War of Independence, creating several drawings of naval battles between the French Navy and the British Royal Navy. After returning to Vevey in 1783, he transformed his battle sketches into oil paintings and watercolours, which earned him a living through drawing lessons. Between 1795 and 1797, Dumoulin was in Paris, where he studied anatomy, copied ancient paintings in the Louvre, attended the Academy and the School of naval constructions. Two of his naval battle paintings were exhibited at the 1796 Salon. Returning to Vevey in 1797, he established a class in technical drawing. In 1810, Dumoulin published a collection of 150 engravings based on the journey of Robinson Crusoe, which is regarded as a precursor to modern comics.[1]
